state.misconception_label: Struggles to visualise nets of 3D shapes

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This is the net of a... ![A circle touching a sector](). I got Triangle because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you are wrapping a gift with wrapping paper. The net of a 3D shape is like the unfolded wrapping paper - it shows how the 3D shape would look if it were flattened out. Just like how you need to consider the whole gift, not just one side, when wrapping, you need to consider the entire 3D shape when identifying its net.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so I need to think about all the pieces together, not just look at one bit? So like, if I unfold a box, all the sides would be the net? But I'm still confused about that circle and sector thing - how do those pieces actually fold up together to make a shape?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you are making a paper cone by cutting and folding a circle. Just like how the circle transforms into a cone, the circle and sector in the net of a 3D shape can fold up to create a specific 3D shape, like a triangular-based pyramid. Each piece plays a crucial role in forming the final shape, just like each side of the wrapping paper matters when wrapping a gift.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses generic analogies rather than addressing the specific circle-and-sector net visualization problem, provides inaccurate information (a circle and sector don't form a triangular pyramid), and the student remains confused by Turn 2 with no evidence of improved understanding.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently grounds every explanation in concrete, everyday analogies (wrapping gifts, making paper cones) that connect the abstract concept of nets to tangible real-world experiences the student can relate to.
